stances.claim: Constitutional martial law need not be feared -- the 1987 Constitution's safeguards (rebellion/invasion-only grounds, 60-day limit, congressional and SC review, no habeas corpus or Bill of Rights suspension) make it a manageable emergency measure.

Defense Secretary Lorenzana and AFP Chief Año are aware of the constitutional limits of Mindanao ML and have carefully observed them -- Lorenzana is a gentleman who knows he will be judged by history.

Authoritarian rule -- where the Constitution is ignored and the head of state governs alone -- must be guarded against; it obliterates the Bill of Rights, abolishes Congress and the SC, and abrogates checks and balances.
On Cha-cha: the author takes neither yes nor no because there are still no details on the specific federal model -- and the possibilities include abolishing the presidency, Congress, and the Senate.
stances.rhetorical_move: principled suspension of judgment pending specifics

stances.claim: ML is not evil per se -- if it were, the 1987 Constitution would have prohibited rather than merely restricted it.

notable_anecdotes: The author observing the September 11 and 21 rallies from the United States -- giving him a detached perspective on the anti-ML passion in Philippine streets.

The 72-hour vs 36-hour detention distinction: the only immediate adverse effect of constitutional ML on ordinary citizens -- and even this requires a simultaneous suspension of the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus.

The author's personal conversations with Defense Secretary Lorenzana -- convinced he is 'a gentleman determined to honor these limits' who 'knows that he is being watched by our people and that he will eventually be judged by history.'
Federalism as 'as novel as a revolutionary government' -- a rhetorical equation linking Cha-cha's radicalism to RevGov-level disruption without the illegality.

one_paragraph_summary: Observing the September rallies (September 11 for Marcos's 100th birthday; September 21 for the 45th ML anniversary) from the United States, Panganiban takes three positions. First, yes to constitutional martial law: the 1987 Constitution has adequately restricted ML to suppressing actual rebellion or invasion (nothing else) when public safety requires it, with congressional and SC review powers, no suspension of the Bill of Rights, and the only immediate adverse effect being authority to detain suspects for 72 hours (vs the normal 36 hours) -- and only if habeas corpus is also suspended. Defense Secretary Lorenzana and AFP Chief Año, administering Mindanao ML, are personally aware of these limits and have observed them; the author finds Lorenzana a genuine gentleman who knows he will be judged by history. ML is not evil per se -- if it were, the 1987 Constitution would have prohibited rather than merely restricted it. Second, no to authoritarian rule: the scenario where the President, backed by the military, sets aside the Constitution and governs alone -- or where a military coup installs a new regime -- obliterates the Bill of Rights, abolishes Congress and the SC, and abrogates all checks and balances. Duterte has recently said he respects and will always follow the Constitution. Third, neither yes nor no to Cha-cha: the author has no position yet because no specific federal model has been presented; the Philippines has no experience with anything but centralized government since the Spanish colonization; and Cha-cha could also abolish the presidency, Congress, and the Senate, cut all official terms, and alter the Bill of Rights -- making it 'as novel as a revolutionary government.'
